title: Complete Guide to US State Privacy Laws
metaDescription: Navigate the complex landscape of US state privacy laws. Compare Texas, Virginia, Colorado laws and stay compliant across multiple states.
intro: With no comprehensive federal privacy law, US states are creating their own data protection regulations. This guide breaks down key state privacy laws including CCPA, Texas TDPSA, Virginia CDPA, and Colorado CPA to help you understand your rights and compliance obligations.
prerequisites: Basic understanding of data privacy concepts
Knowledge of what constitutes personal information
Awareness of your business operations across different states

steps.title: Understand the Current State Privacy Law Landscape
steps.description: Get familiar with the patchwork of state privacy laws currently in effect and upcoming legislation across the United States.
actions: Review which states have comprehensive privacy laws in effect
Identify states where your business operates or has customers
Note effective dates for recently passed legislation
Bookmark state attorney general websites for updates
steps.proTip: Create a spreadsheet tracking all states relevant to your business with their privacy law status and key dates.

steps.title: Master California's CCPA and CPRA Requirements
steps.description: California's Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA) and its amendment (CPRA) set the gold standard for state privacy laws and influence other state legislation.
actions: Study CCPA's definition of personal information and sensitive data
Understand consumer rights: know, delete, correct, opt-out, non-discrimination

Learn the thresholds: annual gross revenue over $25 million, adjusted for inflation to $26,625,000 on January 1, 2025; buying, selling or sharing the data of 100,000+ consumers or households; or 50%+ of revenue from selling or sharing
Review CPRA enhancements including risk assessments and data minimization
steps.proTip: Under the CCPA regulations, businesses must treat a Global Privacy Control signal as a valid request to opt out of sale or sharing; the Attorney General's 2022 settlement with Sephora turned partly on ignoring it.

steps.title: Navigate Virginia's Consumer Data Protection Act (VCDPA)
steps.description: Virginia's law applies to businesses conducting business in Virginia or targeting Virginia residents. It sets no revenue floor: the triggers are consumer counts and revenue from selling personal data.
actions: Check if you meet the threshold: control/process data of 100,000+ consumers or 25,000+ consumers plus 50%+ revenue from data sales
Understand Virginia's consumer rights: access, correct, delete, portability, opt-out
Review data protection assessment requirements for high-risk processing
Implement privacy policy requirements specific to Virginia law
steps.warning: Virginia gives a 30-day cure period after the attorney general's notice, and it does not sunset. Colorado's 60-day cure period did: it expired on January 1, 2025.

steps.title: Comply with the Colorado Privacy Act (CPA)
steps.description: Colorado's law closely mirrors Virginia's approach but includes some unique provisions for data protection assessments and consumer rights.
actions: Verify applicability: 100,000+ Colorado consumers in a calendar year, or 25,000+ if you get revenue or a discount from selling personal data
Understand universal opt-out mechanism requirements
Implement data protection assessment procedures for high-risk processing
Set up processes for consumer request verification and response
steps.proTip: Colorado requires honoring universal opt-out signals, so ensure your website can detect and respond to these browser signals.

steps.title: Prepare for Texas Data Privacy and Security Act (TDPSA)
steps.description: Texas's comprehensive privacy law took effect on July 1, 2024. It sets no revenue or consumer-count threshold: it covers any business that is not a small business under the US Small Business Administration's size standards.
actions: Assess applicability: the act reaches you if you do business in Texas or sell to Texans, process or sell personal data, and are not an SBA-defined small business
Review Texas-specific consumer rights including data portability and correction
Check Texas's separate biometric statute (the Capture or Use of Biometric Identifier Act) if you capture fingerprints, voiceprints or face geometry
Prepare for data processing agreements with third parties

steps.title: Track Emerging State Privacy Legislation
steps.description: Connecticut, Utah, Iowa, Indiana, Tennessee and Montana have all enacted comprehensive privacy laws, and more states pass them each session.
actions: Monitor state legislature websites for privacy bill introductions
Join industry associations that track privacy legislation
Set up Google Alerts for state privacy law news
Follow privacy law attorneys and consultants on social media
Subscribe to privacy law newsletters and publications
steps.proTip: Many states model their laws after Virginia's CDPA, so understanding Virginia's framework helps you quickly adapt to new state laws.

steps.title: Develop a Multi-State Compliance Strategy
steps.description: Create a unified approach to handle multiple state privacy law requirements efficiently while avoiding conflicts between different state requirements.
actions: Map out overlapping requirements across applicable states
Identify the most restrictive requirements to create a baseline compliance program
Develop standardized privacy policies that address all applicable state requirements
Create consumer request handling procedures that work across all states
Establish vendor management processes for multi-state compliance
steps.warning: Some state laws conflict with others - for example, data retention requirements may vary, so legal counsel is often necessary.

pro_tips: Start with the most restrictive state law that applies to your business - often California's CCPA/CPRA - and build your compliance program from there.
Use privacy management platforms that can handle multiple state law requirements simultaneously rather than building separate systems for each state.

Test your own opt-out flow as a customer would: send a request, visit your site with Global Privacy Control turned on in a browser that supports it (Firefox, Brave or DuckDuckGo), and check that ad and analytics tags stop firing.
Implement universal opt-out signal detection even if not required in all states - it's becoming a standard expectation across state laws.
Regular legal reviews are essential as state privacy laws are frequently updated and new states are passing comprehensive privacy legislation each year.

faqs.question: Do I need to comply with every state privacy law if I operate nationally?
faqs.answer: You only need to comply with state privacy laws where you meet the specific thresholds (revenue, number of consumers, etc.) and conduct business or target residents. However, many businesses find it easier to implement the most restrictive requirements across all operations.

faqs.question: What's the difference between state privacy laws and federal laws like HIPAA?
faqs.answer: Federal laws like HIPAA apply to specific industries (healthcare), while state privacy laws are comprehensive and apply to businesses across industries that meet certain thresholds. State laws often provide broader consumer rights.

faqs.question: How do I handle conflicting requirements between different state laws?
faqs.answer: When state laws conflict, you typically must comply with the most restrictive requirement. For complex conflicts, especially around data retention or sharing requirements, consult with privacy attorneys familiar with multi-state compliance.

faqs.question: Are there penalties for non-compliance with state privacy laws?
faqs.answer: Yes, penalties vary by state. California's are adjusted for inflation and have stood at $2,663 per violation and $7,988 per intentional violation, or one involving a consumer known to be under 16, since January 1, 2025. Virginia and Texas cap at $7,500 per violation and both still give a 30-day cure period; Colorado's cure period expired on January 1, 2025, and its violations carry up to $20,000 each as deceptive trade practices. Most states allow only attorney general enforcement, not private lawsuits.

faqs.question: How often do state privacy laws change?
faqs.answer: State privacy laws are rapidly evolving. Existing laws receive amendments annually, and 10+ states introduce new comprehensive privacy bills each legislative session. Regular monitoring is essential for compliance.

faqs.question: Should small businesses worry about state privacy laws?
faqs.answer: Most have thresholds that leave small businesses out, but they are not all revenue-based. California uses revenue ($25 million, adjusted for inflation) or 100,000 consumers or households; Virginia and Colorado use consumer counts only; Texas exempts businesses that meet the US Small Business Administration's size standards. If you sell personal data, those counts drop sharply.
